newsitem.title: FRANCE: French prosecutor to probe Paris region graft.
newsitem.headline: French prosecutor to probe Paris region graft.

text.p: A prosecutor opened an investigation on Tuesday into suspected graft over public works contracts by the Paris regional council, led by an ally of conservative President Jacques Chirac, two days after the left won power in France.

Judicial sources said the Paris public prosecutor's office launched the investigation into the Ile de France council, led by Michel Giraud, for "favouritism, fraud, forgery, receiving the proceeds of fraud and anti-competitive practices in public tenders".
Giraud is a senior member of the Gaullist RPR party of Chirac, who was mayor of Paris until his election as president in 1995.
The investigation targeted "persons unknown", a legal device enabling a magistrate to determine who, if anyone, should be brought to trial for suspected offences.

Sleaze was a major issue in the National Assembly election campaign, with the left accusing Chirac of calling the election almost 10 months early to pre-empt mounting scandals affecting his own party.
Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin officially took over as prime minister on Tuesday after the left won an upset victory in Sunday's runoff votes.
A regional auditors' report sent to Giraud on April 8 condemned "practices aimed at restraining competition", especially in awards of building high schools in the Ile de France region.
But the Paris prosecutor, Gabriel Bestard, had put off an immediate decision on whether to open a probe.
The Greens group in the regional council complained last year that Giraud's council had awarded a string of contracts to a single consultancy firm, Patrimoine Ingenierie, from 1989-94.
It said 171 of 212 such consultancy contracts went to the company, worth a total of 319.5 million francs ($54 million).
In a string of scandals involving awards of public contracts and politics in France, rake-offs are suspected of going back into party coffers. All major parties have been tainted by corruption.
A dissident Gaullist elected official, Claude-Annick Tissot, also denounced alleged tender-rigging in the Ile de France region before being forced to resign last year.
Separately on Tuesday, the Paris prosecutor's office also decided to extend a police probe into two employees at Giraud's residence in Morsang-sur-Seine.
A Paris taxpayers' group alleged last year that the employees were paid by public funds when they were carrying out private duties for Giraud.
